name: Kuji Kiri & Hand Seals
short: The nine seals, mudras and the hand signs from anime
title: Kuji Kiri & Japanese Hand Seals · Real Meaning and History
description: Kuji Kiri, Kuji-in and the mudras of esoteric Buddhism: where the nine seals come from, what they mean, and how they ended up in Naruto and Jujutsu Kaisen. By Dr. Mark Hosak.
dek: You've seen the hand signs in Naruto and Jujutsu Kaisen. Here's the tradition they came from.
intro:
Nine characters, 臨兵闘者皆陣列在前, nine hand positions and nine short mantras. That is the outer shape of Kuji Kiri, the practice of the nine seals. Most people in the West meet it on a screen first, usually as a ninja trick. In Japan it has a much longer and much stranger history.

The earliest sources come from China. Over the centuries the material reached Japan in several waves, through the constant exchange with the mainland, and Japan kept working on it for centuries more. What came out of that is a system you only find in Japan: a combination of Daoism, Japanese folk magic and the esoteric Buddhism of Shingon (mikkyō), carried along by the mountain ascetics of Shugendō and closely tied to Shintō.

In this section I write about that history, about the mudras of esoteric Buddhism, and about the hand signs you know from anime and what they actually point to. You won't find how-to instructions here. The practice itself is passed on in person, and that's where it belongs.

name: Anime → Real Japan
short: What's really behind Naruto, JJK, Demon Slayer and more
title: Anime → Real Japan · The Traditions Behind Naruto, JJK and Demon Slayer
description: Naruto's hand signs, Jujutsu Kaisen's domain expansions, Demon Slayer's Hinokami Kagura: Japanologist Dr. Mark Hosak traces what anime borrowed from real Japanese religion and folklore.
dek: You've seen it in Naruto. Here's the actual text it came from.
list_heading: From the screen to the source
intro:
Japanese creators have always helped themselves from their own tradition. A mudra here, a fox spirit there, a dance that used to be performed for the kami. For a Japanese viewer much of this is background noise, something you grow up with. For everyone else it can be the first glimpse of a very old world.

In this section I take one series at a time and ask a simple question: what did the author actually use, and what does it mean in Japan? Sometimes the answer is surprisingly close to the source. Sometimes the anime version has very little left in common with it, and that's fine too, because it's fiction. Every article ends where the tradition still lives today, in temples, shrines and mountains you can actually visit.

One note so nobody gets the wrong idea: this site isn't connected to any of the series, studios or publishers. I'm a Japanologist who likes good stories and the real things behind them.

name: Yokai & Kami
short: Foxes, tengu, oni and the spirits of Japan
title: Yokai & Kami · An Encyclopedia of Japanese Spirits
description: Kitsune, tengu, oni, kappa and the kami of Japan: where they come from, how Japan depicts them, and where you can still meet them today. By Japanologist Dr. Mark Hosak.
dek: The spirits of Japan, from the nine-tailed fox to the long-nosed tengu, and what they really meant to the people who told their stories.
intro:
Japan has a word for the strange things that happen at the edge of the village: yōkai (妖怪). And it has a word for the powers people worship at shrines: kami (神). The line between the two isn't always clear. A fox can be a trickster in one story and the messenger of a kami in the next, and the tengu of the mountains started out as dangerous beings and ended up as protectors.

In this section I go through the spirits one by one. Where did the stories come from? How did the old picture scrolls and woodblock masters show them? And where can you still see them in Japan today, carved in stone at a shrine, painted on a festival mask, or sold as a little charm?

The illustrations on these pages are original artwork that follows the traditional Japanese ways of depicting each being.

name: Esoteric Japan
short: Shingon, Shugendō, onmyōdō, amulets and purification
title: Esoteric Japan · Shingon, Shugendō, Onmyōdō and Shinto Magic
description: Esoteric Buddhism (Shingon), Shugendō, onmyōdō and Shinto: Japan's magical and spiritual traditions explained by Dr. Mark Hosak, Japanologist and Shingon practitioner and researcher.
dek: Mountain ascetics, court diviners, paper talismans and the secret teachings of Shingon. The spiritual traditions that Japan's stories keep drawing from.
intro:
The character 密 (mitsu) means secret, or dense, or intimate. It's the first half of mikkyō, the esoteric Buddhism that Kūkai brought from China to Japan in the early ninth century and that lives on in the Shingon school. I spent about three years researching its art, architecture and rituals at Kyoto University, and I still practice it.

Esoteric Japan is bigger than one school, though. In Japan the old is rarely thrown away when something new arrives. It lives on next to it and slowly blends in. So you find Shingon next to Shintō, the mountain practice of Shugendō, the court diviners of onmyōdō with their roots in Chinese Daoism, and a whole world of amulets, talismans and purification rites that ordinary people use every day.

This section explains where these traditions come from and what they mean. How to practice them is a different matter, and that part is passed on in person.

name: Sacred Places
short: Kurama, Fushimi Inari and Japan's places of power
title: Sacred Places of Japan · Shrines, Temples and Mountains of Power
description: Fushimi Inari, Mount Kurama, the Kumano Kodo and the torii gates of Japan, seen as sacred places rather than tourist spots. By Dr. Mark Hosak, who walked all 88 temples of Shikoku.
dek: Shrines, temples, waterfalls and mountains, and why the Japanese have treated them as sacred for over a thousand years.
intro:
Most travel guides tell you how to get to a shrine, when it opens and where to buy the best snacks nearby. That's useful. This section looks at the same places from another angle: why they became sacred, which kami or buddhas are present there, and what people have done there for centuries.

I lived in Kyoto for about three years and spent a lot of that time in temples. I also walked the full Shikoku pilgrimage on foot, all 88 temples, after giving up at Temple 24 on my first try. So some of these places I know quite well, including the parts where your feet hurt.

The places mentioned in the other sections show up here too, Mount Kurama with its tengu, or Fushimi Inari with its foxes, so this section will grow as the rest of the grimoire grows.
